title: Astatine: The Rarest Element on Earth

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [curious] There is an element so rare... that if you searched the entire crust of planet Earth right now, you would find less than one gram of it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: One gram. That's about the weight of a paperclip. Spread across the whole planet.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Its name is astatine. Element eighty-five. Today we're finding out why it's so rare... and whether you could ever get your hands on some. [whispers] Spoiler: probably not.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Astatine sits right here on the periodic table, at the bottom of the halogens. Same family as fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Its cousins are everywhere. Chlorine is in your table salt. Iodine is in your multivitamin. So why is astatine basically... missing?

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: It comes down to the nucleus. An astatine atom crams eighty-five protons into an incredibly tiny space. Protons are all positively charged, and they really don't like each other.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Past a certain size, the strong force holding the nucleus together just can't keep up. Every single isotope of astatine is radioactive. There is no stable version. At all.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And it doesn't hang around. The longest-lived kind, astatine two-ten, has a half-life of about eight hours. The kinds found in nature last a minute at most. Some, a tiny fraction of a second.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: So where does natural astatine even come from? Deep underground, uranium and thorium are slowly decaying, step by step, into lead.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Very occasionally, one of those decays takes a rare side path... and for a brief moment, an atom of astatine exists. Then it decays again. And it's gone.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: That's why there's only around a gram on Earth at any moment. Some estimates say up to an ounce. Either way, it's being made and destroyed constantly, at the same time.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And here's the wild part. No one has ever seen a piece of astatine. If you somehow gathered a visible chunk, the heat from its own radioactivity would vaporize it almost instantly.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [amused] So we don't actually know what it looks like. Scientists predict a dark, shiny, metal-like solid. But nobody has ever laid eyes on it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Even the name fits. Astatine comes from the Greek word astatos, which means unstable.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: When Mendeleev built the periodic table in eighteen sixty-nine, the spot below iodine was empty. Chemists called the missing element eka-iodine. For decades, nobody could find it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Then, in nineteen forty, scientists at Berkeley stopped looking for it... and made it instead.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And that's still how you get astatine today. You make it. In a cyclotron.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: A cyclotron whips alpha particles, which are helium nuclei, around and around until they're moving incredibly fast. Then they slam into a target made of bismuth.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Bismuth has eighty-three protons. An alpha particle brings two more. Eighty-three plus two... eighty-five. Astatine.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: The result is astatine two-eleven, with a half-life of about seven hours. So chemists have to pull it out of the target and use it fast. The clock is literally ticking.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And it's worth the rush. Astatine two-eleven is being tested as a cancer treatment. Attached to a molecule that seeks out tumor cells, it fires alpha particles that only travel a few cell widths. Enough to destroy the cancer cell, while mostly sparing the healthy ones around it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: So, can you get some? Not really. You can't buy astatine. It's made in billionths of a gram, at a handful of research cyclotrons around the world, for scientists and clinical trials.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: If you ever do come into contact with astatine, it will most likely be as a patient in one of those trials. And even then, you'll never see it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [warm] The rarest naturally occurring element on Earth. Made in a flash, gone in hours, and never once seen by human eyes.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: If this blew your mind even a little, subscribe. And tell me in the comments: which element should we cover next?
